newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end sharply lower, led by gold.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end sharply lower, led by gold.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended sharply lower Wednesday, led by gold, which fell for the third straight session after the month-long shortcovering rally by funds ran out of steam late last week.

News of a Swiss plan to set up fund to compensate victims of the Holocaust, financed by selling Swiss National Bank gold reserves, undermined sentiment also and raised the prospect of further European central bank gold sales, traders said.
"The Swiss news was only significant because it again says European central banks are now prepared to sell gold," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.
COMEX April gold ended down $6.10 an ounce at $354.50, after sliding to an eight day low at $352.50. Total estimated volume in COMEX gold was 65,000 contracts, which traders said was high.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $352.70/20, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $354.50 and the New York close Tuesday at $358.60/359.10.

Earlier Wednesday the Swiss government proposed a fund to compensate victims of the Holocaust, financed by the sale of about 40 tonnes of gold a year over 10 years from the Swiss National Bank's (SNB) reserves of about 2,583 tonnes (83.28 milion ounces).

But analysts said a 900 tonnes-a-day market could easily absorb sales of 40 tonnes a year and the sales may not occur for some time as the plan would need a change to the Swiss constitution which could take two years.
The gold market rally of the past month had already begun correcting down anyway in the past few days, traders said.
"The Swiss news was just the straw that broke the camel's back," FIMAT New York trader John Tyree said.
COMEX gold had reached overbought levels on both a standard five-day slow stochastic and nine-day relative strength indicator last week, so this week's sell off was not a surprise, analysts said.

The recovery in gold prices in the past month from three year lows around $336.00 had largely been driven by fund shortcovering, with open interest dropping more than 23,000 lots in two weeks before rising Friday and Monday.
In data released Wednesday, COMEX gold open interest fell a further 5,251 lots to 174,030 contracts Tuesday, the lowest level since last November.
But when the rally ran out of steam just short of a major chart resistance point at $370.00, short sellers were tempted back into the market, traders said.
"A bout of short selling could enter this market, taking prices back down toward $350 in the next few days," CPM Group analysts Ted Kempf said.
Gold fell faster than silver Wednesday, with the spot gold/silver ratio slipping to 67.67, after recovering from a 10 month low at 65.60 seen in mid-February.
COMEX May silver closed down 2.5 cents at $5.245, after falling to $5.170 intraday, its lowest level mid-February 13.
NYMEX April platinum closed down $5.20 an ounce at $384.00, while NYMEX June palladium lost $6.00 an ounce to end at $145.50.
But Russian stocks of platinum and palladium may now be lower than earlier estimated, CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.

Using an econometric model run over 10 years that subtracts domestic production and exports from mine production, CPM Group estimates Russian stockpiles of palladium may now be down to only about two million ounces, while platinum stockpiles may be down to about 500,000 ounces.

Earlier in a 1996 report refiner Johnson Matthey said Russian platinum stockpiles could last another two to three years at the current rate of exports, while palladium stocks were expected to last around five years.

Platinum group metals prices had surged in the past month also, on concerns about Russian supplies following the breakdown of the Russia/Japan contract talks in December and news of a threatened strike at the Norilsk mine.
Russia is the world's largest supplier of palladium and the second largest supplier of platinum, after South Africa.
((-Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641))
